claim_rows: | F01-1 | The review treats high-spin nuclear rotation with a rotating mean field, where nucleonic quantization couples intrinsic structure to rotational motion; it presents TAC as a framework allowing the rotational axis to differ from a density principal axis. | review-background / method-formalism | direct | PDF pp.463-468, Abstract, Introduction and cranking overview | false |

| F01-2 | Experimental rotational-band organization is associated with fast electromagnetic connections, smoothly varying transition energies with spin, and gradually changing transition matrix elements; these are organizing criteria rather than a unique proof of a collective model. | review-background | direct | PDF p.465, rotational-band discussion | false |

| F01-3 | In the rotating frame, the experimental Routhian is related to transition-derived rotational frequency and angular momentum; the review distinguishes kinematic and dynamic moments of inertia, with J^(1)=J/omega and J^(2)=dJ/domega. | method-formalism | direct | PDF p.466, E-prime/Routhian discussion | false |

| F01-4 | The cranking model uses a rotating-frame Hamiltonian H-prime = H - omega dot J and a self-consistent mean-field Routhian h-prime = h - omega dot J. A self-consistent solution couples deformation, quasiparticle configuration, rotational frequency and angular-momentum orientation. | method-formalism | direct | PDF pp.467, 469-471, Secs. II-III | false |

| F01-5 | In a body-fixed description, spontaneous breaking of a discrete symmetry produces oriented mean-field solutions; laboratory states require quantization and symmetry restoration. The review uses this distinction to connect mean-field order parameters with rotational bands. | review-background / author interpretation | direct | PDF pp.473-476, Sec. II.F and symmetry discussion | false |

| F01-6 | Principal-axis rotation preserves a signature-like discrete operation and commonly yields Delta I=2 sequences. Planar tilted-axis rotation breaks the corresponding symmetry and can produce a Delta I=1 sequence together with signature-partner behavior. | model-result / review-background | direct | PDF pp.475-476, Sec. III.B | false |

| F01-7 | In a triaxial planar solution, two Delta I=2 sequences can merge into a Delta I=1 band as the tilt develops; the review presents this as a possible triaxiality clue, not as a model-independent experimental criterion. | author interpretation | direct | PDF pp.475-476 and p.504, conclusion | false |

| F01-8 | An aplanar TAC solution has angular momentum components outside the principal planes. The two opposite-handed mean-field solutions are related by a discrete symmetry and combine, after laboratory-frame restoration, into two same-parity near-degenerate Delta I=1 bands. | model-result / review-background | direct | PDF pp.476, 484-485 and p.504 | false |

| F01-9 | The review contrasts TAC's semiclassical mean-field geometry with PRM or related quantum treatments: TAC does not by itself describe quantum tunneling between left- and right-handed configurations or guarantee good total angular momentum, while PRM can calculate quantum spectra and transition strengths only within its assumed core deformation and configuration space. | method-formalism / limitation | direct | PDF pp.484-485; Sec. III.C; discussion of PRM comparison | false |

| F01-10 | Magnetic rotation is described as rotation of high-j particle and hole current loops in a nearly spherical mass distribution. The shears mechanism closes the particle and hole blades, increases angular momentum, and produces large M1 strength with small E2 strength; the transverse magnetic moment and its decrease along a band are central observables. | review-background / author interpretation | direct | PDF pp.487-488, Fig. 18 and Sec. IV.A | false |

| F01-11 | Antimagnetic rotation uses two shears arranged so that their transverse magnetic moments largely cancel. The review associates this with regular Delta I=2 bands, very small B(E2), and a large J^(2)/B(E2) ratio; the orientation is mainly a current-distribution effect rather than a large charge deformation. | review-background / model-result | direct | PDF p.488, Fig. 19 and Sec. IV.A | false |

| F01-12 | Band termination is interpreted as progressive alignment of available valence angular momenta until the mean field approaches rotational symmetry about J; further spin then requires a particle-hole excitation and can interrupt the regular sequence. Deformation, moments of inertia and symmetry-breaking indicators may change along the terminating path. | review-background / model-result | direct | PDF pp.492-495 and p.505, Sec. V and Conclusions | false |

| F01-13 | Reflection-asymmetric mean fields have finite electric octupole and, where not cancelled, electric dipole moments as order parameters. Fast E3 or E1 transitions and parity-doublet patterns are discussed as consequences of the assumed symmetry type, not as proof that every such band has a stable octupole minimum. | review-background / method-formalism | direct | PDF pp.495-498, Sec. VI | false |

| F01-14 | The review identifies beyond-mean-field corrections as necessary for tunneling, band mixing, symmetry restoration and collective fluctuations. It discusses shell-model/projection methods, RPA, and generator-coordinate approaches; RPA is also presented as a route to wobbling and low-lying chiral-vibration modes near a mean-field solution. | review-background / limitation | direct | PDF pp.499-502, Sec. VIII | false |

| F01-15 | The conclusions distinguish PAC, planar TAC, aplanar/chiral rotation, magnetic rotation, antimagnetic rotation and reflection-asymmetric rotation by their symmetry content and dominant observables, while emphasizing open questions about realistic interactions, coupling between orientations and the transition from quantal current-loop rotation to classical collective rotation. | author synthesis / future-proposal | direct | PDF pp.503-505, Sec. X | false |
